title: Defining the Scale in Performance Ratings
hook: Same observation. A 4 and a 2. The spread is not about the teacher. It is about the scale.
counterintuition: Rating scales assign numbers to performance, but unless each level is defined by observable behaviors, each rater supplies their own private definition of each number. When they apply those private definitions to the same subject, the spread includes two layers: disagreement about performance, and disagreement about what the numbers mean. The second layer is about the scale, not the subject. It disappears when each level is defined by what can be observed.
tryThisNow: Find a rating scale you use. Write one observable behavior that would distinguish the middle level from the level above it. If you describe a mindset instead of an action, the scale is not anchored.
keyTakeaway: Unanchored rating scales let raters supply private definitions of each level, producing noise from scale interpretation on top of real performance differences. Behavioral anchors remove the scale-interpretation layer.

breakdown.fastRead:
Two principals watch the same classroom observation video. One rates instructional quality a 4. The other rates it a 2. Both reference the same moments to explain their scores. The moments are not the source of the disagreement. The absence of a shared definition of what a 3 looks like is.

A scale that assigns numbers to levels without describing observable behaviors for each level creates two kinds of noise: disagreement about the subject, and disagreement about what the scale levels mean. The first is information. The second is scale design. The spread across raters includes both, and they cannot be separated unless each level is defined.
breakdown.deepRead:
Walk through a performance review with two raters and a single subject. Both raters receive the same information about the subject's work and the same 1-to-5 rating scale. Their scores differ. Ask each rater to explain the gap. Often, what surfaces is not a disagreement about the subject's behaviors but a disagreement about the scale: what a 3 means in this context, and what earns a 4 versus a 5.

Consider the middle points of any unanchored scale. The endpoints produce more agreement without definition: a 1 is clearly unacceptable, a 5 is clearly outstanding, and raters roughly agree on extreme cases. But the middle points are where most subjects fall, and they have the least definitional content. A 3 out of 5 for communication skills could mean anything from the employee sends clear written communications to the employee presents to clients without a script. The rater supplies the definition. If five raters supply five different definitions of 3, the spread in their ratings tells you nothing about the employee. It tells you about the five private definitions. Research on behaviorally anchored rating scales has consistently shown that rater agreement improves when each scale level is defined by observable behavioral descriptions rather than numbers or generic adjectives, and that the improvement is most pronounced at the middle scale points where interpretation diverges most.

Adding more scale points to an unanchored scale does not improve precision. It adds more undefined middle space. Precision comes from the specificity of the level definitions, not from the number of levels.

The inter-rater agreement statistic measures both rater disagreement and scale vagueness in a single number.
breakdown.fullRead:
The hum of a classroom on the projection screen fills the conference room where Norman is running the calibration exercise. Both principals have watched the same 15-minute observation video. He collects their rating sheets before they discuss. Instructional quality: 4 and 2, on a 5-point scale. Norman reads both sets of notes aloud. Both principals flagged the moment where the teacher paused for student responses. One rated it excellent formative assessment practice, placing the teacher at a 4. The other rated the same pause as inadequate wait time before the teacher redirected, placing the teacher at a 2. The notes reference the same second of the same video. The scale does not contain a definition of what a 3 looks like that either principal could compare their interpretation against.

The research tradition on behaviorally anchored rating scales developed from a straightforward observation: rating scales that define each level by specific observable behaviors produce higher inter-rater agreement than scales that use generic adjectives or numbers alone. The key finding is about where agreement breaks down without anchoring: raters at the scale extremes show reasonable agreement because extreme levels are legible without definition. Raters at the middle levels disagree significantly because the middle levels require the most interpretive work. Behavioral anchors do not improve precision by defining the obvious. They improve precision by resolving the space where private definitions currently diverge.

'My unit averages 3.8 on clinical competence,' Millicent says. 'Mine averages 2.6,' says Julian. Both managers are looking at peer review data from comparable nursing populations. The gap looks like a performance difference between the two units. When Norman facilitates the follow-up question, it turns out to be something else: Millicent's unit uses follows protocol independently as the behavioral reference for a 3, while Julian's unit uses teaches protocol to new staff. In Millicent's implicit definition, a 3 is a competent nurse. In Julian's, a 3 is a mentor. The scores are accurate to their private anchors and meaningless when placed in the same column.

Clarence discovers the calibration problem when two senior engineers score the same pull request a 4 and a 2 on the same day. Both reviewers identified the same issue in their comments: insufficient edge case handling. The disagreement is not about whether the issue exists. It is about where on the scale it belongs. One reviewer treats unresolved edge case handling as a concern that reduces the rating to a 2. The other treats the same issue as a concern that still allows a 4. Neither has a written definition of what separates a 2 from a 4 for this type of issue. The scale was designed as a quality signal. It has been functioning as a private judgment mapped onto a shared number.

When you use a scale with undefined middle levels, you are not measuring the subject. You are measuring the interaction between the subject's behaviors and your private definition of each level. A different rater with a different private definition produces a different score for the same subject. The spread across raters includes both components: some genuine disagreement about what the subject does, and some definitional noise from the scale. Behavioral anchors are not a constraint on rater judgment. They are a way of separating the two components so the genuine disagreement can be heard.

An inter-rater agreement of 0.41 on a use-of-force proportionality scale is barely above chance. Percival finds that when supervisors discuss their divergent ratings, the disagreements cluster at the middle scale points. His diagnosis is not that the supervisors need more training. The middle scale points have no behavioral anchor. The noise is in the scale, not the supervisors. The scale is where the fix belongs.

memorableLines.text: The first is information. The second is scale design.
memorableLines.why: Two sentences, two words each for the predicate: labels the distinction between the noise sources as efficiently as possible, making the two-layer structure stick.

memorableLines.text: The rater supplies the definition. If five raters supply five different definitions of 3, the spread in their ratings tells you nothing about the employee.
memorableLines.why: The two-sentence structure moves from mechanism to implication: names who is doing the defining (the rater, not the scale) and then names what that means for interpretation (the spread is about the raters, not the employee).

memorableLines.text: The noise is in the scale, not the supervisors. The scale is where the fix belongs.
memorableLines.why: Redirects the diagnosis from person to process in two short sentences, turning the chapter's core argument into a concrete next action.

examples.title: Same Moment, Different Frame

planSpec.domain: teacher performance review: two principals rating the same classroom observation video using an unanchored 1-5 scale
planSpec.audience: a school district quality manager comparing ratings before and after anchor-definition training
planSpec.stakes: teacher career decisions and professional development allocation ��� noisy ratings mean support goes to the wrong teachers
planSpec.requiredBeat: the district manager plays a 15-minute classroom observation video to both principals independently: one rates it a 4 on instructional quality; the other rates it a 2; when asked to explain, they describe the same specific moments with different evaluative frames, and neither has a shared definition of what a 3 looks like

examples.scenario: The 15-minute classroom observation video plays in the conference room. Norman collects the rating sheets before either principal speaks. Instructional quality: 4, from one; 2, from the other. Norman reads both sets of notes aloud. Both principals described the same moment: the teacher's pause before redirecting a student question. One read it as formative assessment. The other read it as lost wait time. The scale has five levels and no definition of what a 3 requires in observable terms. Both ratings are defensible. Neither is comparable.
examples.whatToDo: Before any rating session involving multiple raters, define each scale level in observable behavioral terms. For instructional quality, describe what actions a teacher would be taking that place their lesson at a 3 versus a 4. The anchor is a behavior the rater could report seeing, not a judgment the rater is left to infer.
examples.whyItMatters: A 2-point gap for the same observation, with both raters citing the same moment, shows that the spread is not evidence of a teacher quality difference. It is evidence of a scale definition gap that the two raters filled with different private interpretations.

examples.title: 3.8 vs. 2.6

planSpec.domain: nurse peer review: a hospital using a 1-to-5 clinical competence scale with no behavioral definitions across three nursing units
planSpec.audience: a nursing director comparing peer review scores across units for the same competency category
planSpec.stakes: consistent professional development support and fair employment decisions — if clinical competence means different things across units, the peer reviews are not comparable
planSpec.requiredBeat: two nursing managers compare their units' clinical competence distributions: one unit averages 3.8 and the other 2.6 for comparable nursing populations; when the managers discuss their definitions of a 3, they discover they have been anchoring the scale to completely different observable behaviors

examples.scenario: 'My unit averages 3.8 on clinical competence,' Millicent says. 'Mine averages 2.6,' Julian replies. Both managers review peer assessments for comparable nursing populations. The gap looks like a performance difference. Julian asks what a 3 means to Millicent: follows protocol independently. Millicent asks what a 3 means to Julian: teaches protocol to new staff. A 3 is a competent nurse in one unit. In the other, it is a mentor. The scale scores have been measuring two different things under the same number.
examples.whatToDo: Before aggregating peer review scores across teams or units, verify that raters in each group are applying the same behavioral anchor to each level. Numerical comparisons across units are not valid until the level definitions are shared.
examples.whyItMatters: The 1.2-point gap between the two units disappears as a performance finding once the behavioral definitions diverge. The scale was producing a fictional comparison that looked meaningful only because both units used the same number.

examples.title: 4 and 2 for the Same Issue

planSpec.domain: software code review: an engineering team rating code quality on a 1-to-4 scale for six months before discovering the scale means different things to different reviewers
planSpec.audience: an engineering manager who discovers the team's code quality scores are not calibrated across reviewers
planSpec.stakes: technical debt and product quality decisions — code quality scores that mean different things to different reviewers produce inconsistent merge decisions
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager realizes the calibration problem when two senior engineers review the same pull request on the same day and score it a 4 and a 2; both identified the same issue in their comments; the scale has no written definition for what unresolved edge case handling implies for each level

examples.scenario: Six months into using the 1-to-4 code quality scale, Clarence notices two senior engineers have scored the same pull request a 4 and a 2 on the same day. He pulls the review comments. Both engineers identified the same issue: insufficient edge case handling. The disagreement is not about whether the issue exists. It is about where on the scale insufficient edge case handling belongs. Each engineer has been applying a private threshold. Neither has a written definition to compare theirs against. The scale has been recording private thresholds, not a shared quality standard.
examples.whatToDo: When two experienced reviewers score the same artifact very differently while citing the same issues, suspect a scale definition gap before attributing the difference to rater judgment or expertise. Workshop explicit level definitions for the issue types that appear most often in reviews.
examples.whyItMatters: Identical issues producing a 4 and a 2 from experienced reviewers shows the scale is not measuring code quality: it is recording each reviewer's private mapping of a specific issue type to a number. Two such maps produce no comparable signal.

planSpec.domain: police body-camera footage review: a police department using a use-of-force proportionality scale across three supervisors
planSpec.audience: a police standards officer comparing supervisor ratings of the same footage samples
planSpec.stakes: consistent accountability and officer development — supervisors with different implicit definitions of proportionality produce inconsistent ratings that undermine accountability and officer trust
planSpec.requiredBeat: the standards officer asks the three supervisors to rate the same six body-camera clips independently: inter-rater agreement is 0.41; when the supervisors discuss their ratings, disagreements cluster at the middle scale points where the behavioral anchor is most vague

examples.scenario: If three supervisors rate six identical body-camera clips on a use-of-force proportionality scale, what would inter-rater agreement look like? Percival reveals the exercise result: 0.41, barely above chance. The discussion after the exercise tells the more important story: the disagreements cluster at the middle scale points. The extreme cases produce rough agreement. The cases that fall in the proportionality band between clearly appropriate and clearly excessive are where the scale's lack of a behavioral definition generates most of the spread. Middle-scale cases are also the most common. The scale is noisiest where the work is hardest.
examples.whatToDo: When conducting a scale calibration exercise, pay particular attention to which scale levels produce the most inter-rater variation. Those levels need behavioral anchor definitions first. Calibration training that does not resolve the definitional gap only produces temporary agreement from discussion, not structural reduction in scale noise.
examples.whyItMatters: An inter-rater agreement of 0.41 with disagreements concentrated at the middle levels shows that the scale's vagueness is worst exactly where the most cases land. The scale is producing the most noise where it matters most.

examples.title: Four Verdict-Changing Cases

planSpec.domain: financial advisor compliance audit: a brokerage reviewing suitability assessment scores across five compliance officers for the same client profiles
planSpec.audience: a compliance director studying inter-officer consistency in suitability ratings
planSpec.stakes: regulatory compliance and client protection — inconsistent suitability ratings mean some clients receive unsuitable product recommendations depending on which officer reviewed the file
planSpec.requiredBeat: you are reviewing the calibration exercise results: across 20 client profiles rated by all five officers, the standard deviation within each profile is 0.9 points on a 5-point scale; the spread crosses the suitable/unsuitable threshold in four of the twenty cases; the culprit is the investment sophistication category, which has no behavioral anchor

examples.scenario: Your compliance team's calibration exercise results are on your desk. Twenty client profiles, five officers, standard deviation of 0.9 points per profile on the 5-point suitability scale. Four profiles show spread that crosses the suitable/unsuitable threshold: the same client profile produces a suitable verdict from two officers and unsuitable from two others. The fifth officer is split from both groups. The investment sophistication category is the driver: each officer is applying their own implicit definition of what intermediate investment experience looks like in observable terms. The decision about whether a client is suitable for a product is changing based on which officer reads the file.
examples.whatToDo: Identify the specific scale categories driving the most inter-officer variance in calibration exercises. Define those categories with observable behavioral criteria (client described specific portfolio strategies versus client expressed familiarity with investment products generally) before the next review cycle begins.
examples.whyItMatters: Four verdict-changing profiles out of twenty, traced to one unanchored category, shows that scale vagueness in one critical dimension is producing material inconsistency in compliance outcomes. The client's protection should not depend on which officer reviews the file.

examples.title: Seven Points

planSpec.domain: restaurant critic scoring criteria: a food publication comparing three critics' scores on the same restaurant experience using an unanchored 1-to-10 scale
planSpec.audience: a food publication editor studying whether the critic scoring system is producing comparable scores across writers
planSpec.stakes: publication credibility — if critics are applying different implicit standards, a restaurant's final score depends on who reviewed it rather than on the restaurant's quality
planSpec.requiredBeat: the editor compares the three critics' scores for the same blind tasting: food quality was rated 7, 9, and 6; service was rated 8, 5, and 7; ambiance was rated 9, 6, and 8; the spread produces possible composite scores from 19 to 26 for the same visit; each critic uses a different reference point to define a 7

examples.scenario: The scoring summary for the blind tasting sits on Mabel's desk. Three critics, one restaurant visit, three columns. Food quality: 7, 9, 6. Service: 8, 5, 7. Ambiance: 9, 6, 8. Possible composite scores range from 19 to 26 for the same meal. Mabel asks each critic what a 7 for food quality means. Three answers: a menu that executes competently on an established concept; a meal with a memorable dish among otherwise workmanlike execution; a kitchen that shows technique without originality. Each answer is defensible. None is shared. The scale is not measuring the restaurant. It is measuring each critic's private reference point.
examples.whatToDo: Before using a numeric scale across multiple reviewers for the same subject, define what each critical level number means in terms of observable food, service, or other characteristics. A 7 in food quality should describe specific observable food attributes, not evaluative impressions that each critic translates privately.
examples.whyItMatters: A seven-point composite range for the same meal, produced by three experienced critics using the same scale, shows that the scale is recording private anchors rather than a shared measurement. The restaurant's score becomes a function of which critic showed up.

questions.prompt: What is 'scale noise' in the context of performance rating?
choices: The variation in ratings that results from raters using the same scale at different points in time rather than simultaneously.
The variation in ratings that results from raters applying different private definitions of what each scale level means, independent of actual performance differences.
The variation in ratings that results from raters comparing the subject to different reference groups within the same organization.
questions.explanation: Scale noise is the component of rating variance that comes from scale interpretation, not performance differences. It arises when each rater supplies a private definition of each level because the scale does not provide one.

questions.prompt: Two principals rate the same classroom observation video a 4 and a 2 on a 5-point instructional quality scale. Both reference the same moments in their written notes. What is the most direct diagnosis?
choices: The scale does not define what the middle levels look like, so the two principals are applying different private definitions of what a 4 and a 2 require.
The principals have different levels of expertise in classroom observation, producing different interpretations of the same instructional events.
The principals are using different reference classes: one compares to the best teachers and the other to average teachers in the district.
questions.explanation: Both principals referenced the same moments but reached different evaluative conclusions. The moments themselves did not produce the disagreement. The absence of shared behavioral definitions for the scale levels did.

questions.prompt: A nursing director finds that one unit averages 3.8 and another 2.6 on a clinical competence peer review scale for comparable nursing populations. A follow-up reveals the two managers have been using different behavioral references for a score of 3. What does this finding reveal about the gap?
choices: The gap reflects a real difference in clinical competence between the two nursing units that should inform professional development decisions.

The gap is at least partly an artifact of scale interpretation: the two units have been measuring different behaviors with the same number, making their scores incomparable until the behavioral anchors are shared.
The gap reveals that one manager is systematically more lenient, a bias that anchor training could correct by moving their scores toward the other manager's distribution.
questions.explanation: The two managers were using different observable behaviors to define the same scale level. When the definitions diverge, the numbers are not measuring the same thing and cannot be compared. The gap is an artifact of scale interpretation.

questions.prompt: An engineering team has used a 1-to-4 code quality scale for six months. Two senior engineers score the same pull request a 4 and a 2 on the same day, both citing the same issue. Which improvement most directly addresses the source of the variance?
choices: Provide calibration training so the two engineers understand they should be scoring identical issues identically.
Replace the 4-point scale with a 6-point scale to give engineers more options to distinguish quality levels.
Define observable behavioral criteria for what insufficient edge case handling implies for each scale level, so all engineers apply the same threshold for the same issue type.
questions.explanation: The source of the variance is the absence of a shared definition of what the identified issue implies for each scale level. Behavioral criteria for common issue types provide the shared threshold that the calibration and scale expansion do not.

questions.prompt: Three supervisors rating body-camera footage show an inter-rater agreement of 0.41, with disagreements clustering at the middle scale points of a use-of-force proportionality scale. What does the clustering pattern reveal?
choices: The supervisors have received inconsistent training on use-of-force standards, producing random disagreement across all scale levels.
The middle scale points have the least behavioral definition, producing the most interpretive divergence at the levels where most cases fall and where the behavioral distinction matters most.
The body-camera footage at the middle-scale cases is of lower quality, making accurate assessment harder than at extreme cases.
questions.explanation: Middle scale points have the most interpretive room and the least definitional content. Most real-world cases fall in the middle range, so this is where the scale's vagueness does the most damage to inter-rater consistency.

questions.prompt: A compliance director proposes improving a suitability assessment scale by expanding from 5 to 7 points. Would this change reduce scale noise?
choices: Yes, because more scale points give raters finer distinctions, reducing the chance that two raters map different performance levels to the same number.
Yes, because additional points force raters to be more precise in their thinking, reducing spread through greater cognitive effort.
No, because adding more scale points without adding behavioral definitions for each new point creates more undefined middle space rather than reducing interpretive variation.
questions.explanation: The source of scale noise is the absence of behavioral definitions, not the number of scale points. Expanding the scale without defining each new level adds more undefined space where private definitions can diverge.

questions.prompt: A food publication editor wants to improve consistency across three critics who rate the same restaurants. The critics use an unanchored 1-to-10 scale. Which change most directly reduces scale noise?
choices: Define what a 7, 8, and 9 look like for each category by describing the observable characteristics that earn each score, so each critic applies the same threshold.
Require critics to discuss their scores after independently completing each review so they can identify and resolve disagreements before publication.
Reduce the scale from 10 to 5 points to decrease the number of undefined middle levels where interpretive variation occurs.
questions.explanation: Behavioral definitions for each level are the direct fix for scale noise. Post-review discussion produces temporary agreement from deliberation, which is a form of social convergence rather than structural scale improvement. Reducing scale points without adding definitions merely relocates the undefined middle.

questions.prompt: You are designing a performance review scale for recurring assessment of the same competency across multiple managers. Which feature most directly reduces scale-interpretation noise?
choices: Write a specific observable behavior description for each scale level that distinguishes what a 2 looks like from a 3 and what a 3 looks like from a 4, before any rater uses the scale.
Train raters on the scale by reviewing their scores after each cycle and providing feedback on how closely they align to a reference rater.
Use an even-numbered scale to force raters away from the middle point, where most interpretive noise concentrates.
questions.explanation: Observable behavior descriptions for each level are the direct structural change that reduces interpretive variation. Calibration training after the fact and scale point configuration both leave the definitional gap open at the moment of rating.

questions.prompt: After a behavioral anchor workshop, inter-rater agreement on a teacher performance scale improved from 0.39 to 0.67. A manager argues this improvement proves teachers are being rated more accurately. Is this interpretation correct?
choices: Yes, because higher agreement means raters are more accurately perceiving the teacher's actual performance, which is what the scale measures.
Yes, because behavioral anchors force raters to attend to the same observable behaviors, which filters irrelevant variation and leaves only accuracy-relevant information.

Not necessarily. The improved agreement shows raters are now applying the same scale definitions. Whether those definitions correspond to meaningful performance dimensions is a separate question the agreement statistic does not answer.
questions.explanation: Agreement measures consistency across raters, not accuracy against an external standard. Raters can consistently apply a shared but poorly designed anchor. The improvement in agreement confirms that the scale interpretation layer of noise has been reduced; it does not confirm that what is being measured is the right thing.

reviewCards.front: What is a behaviorally anchored rating scale?
reviewCards.back: A rating scale where each level is defined by observable behavioral descriptions rather than numbers or generic adjectives. Behavioral anchors replace each rater's private definition of a level with a shared definition of what observable actions earn that score.

reviewCards.front: Why do unanchored rating scales generate scale noise independent of rater quality?
reviewCards.back: Without behavioral definitions, each rater supplies a private definition of each level. Those private definitions differ across raters, adding interpretive variation to the rating before any genuine performance disagreement is registered. The noise is in the scale design, not in the raters.

reviewCards.front: Why do middle scale points generate more noise than the endpoints of an unanchored scale?
reviewCards.back: Extreme scale points have enough implicit meaning to produce rough agreement: obviously terrible versus obviously excellent. Middle points have the most interpretive room and the least implicit content, which is where private definitions diverge most. Most subjects fall in the middle range, so this is where the scale does the most damage.

reviewCards.front: Why doesn't adding more scale points improve precision on an unanchored scale?
reviewCards.back: More scale points add more undefined middle space. Precision comes from the specificity of level definitions, not from the number of levels. Expanding from 5 to 7 points without adding behavioral definitions for each new level relocates the definitional gap rather than closing it.

reviewCards.front: What does high inter-rater agreement after anchor training confirm and not confirm?
reviewCards.back: It confirms that the scale-interpretation layer of noise has been reduced: raters are applying the same definitions. It does not confirm that the definitions themselves correspond to meaningful performance dimensions. Agreement is a measure of consistency, not accuracy.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Design rating scales with observable behavioral descriptions for each level before any rater uses the scale. The three-step process is: (1) identify the middle scale point that produces the most interpretive divergence, (2) write what an evaluator would observe in the subject's actual behavior that places them at that level versus one level above and one level below, (3) verify that the description names an observable action rather than an evaluative judgment, and then repeat for each level. The behavioral anchor replaces private definitions with a shared threshold.

ifThenPlans.context: Two experienced raters produce a large score gap for the same subject on the same scale.
ifThenPlans.plan: Before assuming rater bias or expertise differences, ask each rater to define what would place someone at the level they scored. If the definitions diverge on observable behaviors, the gap is a scale design problem. Workshop shared behavioral anchors for the divergent levels before the next rating cycle.

ifThenPlans.context: You are comparing rating scores across teams or units that have been using the same scale independently.
ifThenPlans.plan: Before drawing any conclusions from the comparison, verify that each team was applying the same behavioral anchor to each level. Conduct a calibration exercise: show both groups the same subject and compare their scores. If the scores diverge, the scale is being applied differently across groups and the numbers are not comparable.

ifThenPlans.context: You are building a new rating scale for a recurring judgment in your domain.
ifThenPlans.plan: Draft the behavioral anchor for the middle level first, because it requires the most precision and is where most subjects will be rated. Write what observable behavior distinguishes the middle level from one level above and one level below. Then extend the anchor definitions to the remaining levels. Test the scale with two independent raters on five sample subjects before deploying it. Anchor quality is measured by whether the two raters reach the same score without discussing.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, find one rating scale you use and pick its middle level. Write one sentence describing an observable behavior that would distinguish a subject at that level from a subject one level above it. If your sentence describes an evaluative impression rather than an observable action, the scale is not behaviorally anchored and your ratings are carrying scale interpretation noise in every score.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, take one scale category from a rating instrument your team uses regularly and write behavioral anchor descriptions for at least three of its levels: the middle, one above, and one below. After four weeks, you will have anchored the most important levels in the scales you use most. Run a calibration exercise with a colleague for one of the anchored categories and compare scores. The gap between your scores before and after anchoring is the size of the scale noise the anchors removed.
